info.description:
Share signals - records, documents and events - between the members of Information Sharing Networks.

## Key concepts
- **Information Sharing Network (ISN)**: a network set up for one purpose, such as sharing consignment data between traders, ports and government agencies. Its members are accounts, each with its own access rights (see *Who can see signals*), and it defines the signal types those members can exchange.
- **Signal type**: identified by a slug and a version (e.g. `consignment/v1.0.0`). Each signal type has one of three content kinds: a **json** record typically describes an entity (e.g. a consignment), a **document** is a file (e.g. a certificate PDF), and an **event** records that something happened to another signal (e.g. a certificate was approved). json and event types usually have a JSON schema that the content is checked against. New signal types can be added at any time without affecting existing ones.
- **Signal**: one piece of information shared through an ISN. Each signal belongs to one signal type. json signals and documents can be updated with new versions, while events never change. Signals can be linked to each other, e.g. a consignment's documents and events are linked to the consignment (see *Correlation*).

The examples below use consignments moving through ports, but the service is generic: each network defines its own ISNs, signal types and schemas.

## API documentation
- [/docs](/docs): using the API - authentication, finding ISNs, and submitting and searching signals
- [/admin-docs](/admin-docs): administering the service - ISNs and their permissions, signal types, routing, and accounts
- [/ui-docs](/ui-docs): the browser-based management interface

# Authentication
Protected endpoints need a JWT access token in the Authorization header:
```
Authorization: Bearer <access-token>
```

**Service accounts**
- **Get a token**: `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type=client_credentials`, and the client ID and secret as form fields or HTTP Basic auth.
- **Renew it**: request a new token in the same way.
- **Lifetime**: access tokens last 30 minutes.

**Web users**
- **Get a token**: `POST /api/auth/login` with email and password. The access token is in the response body, and a refresh token is set as an HTTP-only cookie.
- **Renew it**: `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type=refresh_token` (the cookie is sent automatically). The refresh token is rotated.
- **Lifetime**: access tokens last 30 minutes. Refresh tokens last 30 days from the last refresh, so users only log in again after 30 days without using the service.
- **Sessions**: each login or refresh revokes the user's other refresh tokens, so a user has one session at a time. Changing or resetting a password ends the session (the refresh token is revoked), so the user needs to log in again.

For both kinds of account, the access token holds the account's role and ISN permissions when it was issued, so permission changes and disabled accounts take effect when the account next gets a token (within 30 minutes). The admin endpoints check the account's current role and status on every request, so changes apply to them straight away.

# Signals

## Content kinds
Each signal type's `content_kind` decides how its signals are sent:
- **json**: sent with *Submit Signals* or *Submit Signals via Router*. The content is validated against the signal type's schema (unless the type was set up to skip validation).
- **document**: a PDF, JPEG, PNG or XML file, sent with *Upload a Document* or *Upload a Document via Router* and fetched with *Download a Document*. Search results contain the document's metadata, not the file.
- **event**: sent with *Submit Signals*, and validated like json (see *Events* for the extra rules).

Search, withdrawal and batches work the same way for every kind.

## References and versions
A signal describes one thing, such as a consignment or a certificate. When it changes, you send it again and the service stores a new version of the same signal, so recipients see the latest version and its history.
- **`local_ref`**: your reference for the signal, usually its ID in your own system. Send the same `local_ref` every time you send the signal. It is unique for your account, the ISN and the signal type version, so sending the same `local_ref` to two ISNs or two signal types creates two separate signals.
- **`signal_id`**: the service's ID for the signal, given when it is first stored. Other participants use it to refer to your signal, e.g. to link to it (see *Correlation*).
- **`issuer_ref`** (optional, documents only): the reference given by whoever issued the thing the document represents, e.g. an export health certificate number. It doesn't need to be unique. Recipients can find documents with the `issuer_ref` search filter.

When you send a `local_ref` to the same ISN again:
- **If something changed**, a new version is stored.
- **If nothing changed** (the same content, and the same or no `correlation_id`), nothing is stored. The response returns the existing latest version with `unchanged: true`, so requests can be safely retried. JSON is compared as JSON (key order and whitespace are ignored). Documents compare the file, its filename and its `issuer_ref`.
- **If the signal was withdrawn**, it is reactivated with a new version.
- **Events never change**: resending an event with different content or a different `correlation_id`, or after it was withdrawn, fails with `resource_already_exists`. To correct an event, withdraw it and send a new event with a new `local_ref`.

## Correlation
Link a signal to another signal in the same ISN by setting its `correlation_id` to the other signal's `signal_id`. Search results include each signal's `correlation_id` (null if it isn't linked to another signal).
- **Link to the entity directly**: e.g. link a consignment's documents and events to the consignment, not to each other. Correlation is one level deep.
- **Linking is sharing**: linking your signal to another account's signal is like emailing that account a copy, except that they see your later versions, and withdrawing the signal stops their access through the service. If a new version changes the `correlation_id`, access moves with it: the owner of the newly linked signal can see every version, and the previous owner can no longer see it.

## Events
An event records that a process waypoint was reached for the signal it is linked to, e.g. `ehc-approved` (an export health certificate was approved) or `departed-origin`. Each waypoint is its own event type, so recipients choose which events they receive by choosing which event types to search or poll.
- **`correlation_id` is required**: link the event to the signal it is about (e.g. the consignment). Requests containing events without one are rejected.
- **`content` must include `occurred_at`**: when the waypoint was reached, as an RFC 3339 timestamp with a time zone offset (e.g. `2026-09-27T14:02:00Z`).
- **`subject`**: if the event is about a specific version of a signal (e.g. version 3 of a document), name it in a `subject` field in `content`: `{"signal_id": "...", "version": 3}`. Always include the version, as later versions may be different.
- **Order isn't enforced**: events are accepted in any order and can repeat (e.g. several inspections). To build a timeline, order a signal's linked events by `occurred_at`.

**Schemas for event types** validate the event's `content`, as for json types, but:
- the service checks `occurred_at` whatever the schema says. The schema must still allow it: declare `occurred_at` (and `subject`, if the type has one) and list it as required, especially if the schema uses `"additionalProperties": false`
- `occurred_at` and `subject` are reserved - don't use them for anything else
- the service doesn't check `subject` yet, so a type whose events have a subject should require it in its schema, as `{"signal_id": <uuid>, "version": <integer>}`

## Who can see signals
- Accounts with **read** access to an ISN can see every signal in it.
- Accounts with **write-only** access can see the signals they created, and the signals other accounts have linked to their signals (one level deep).
- Signals in a **public** ISN can be searched by anyone, with *Signal Search (public ISNs)* (`/api/public/isn/...`). Downloading a document still needs an access token and access to the ISN.

An account can have different access in each ISN, and searches across several ISNs apply each ISN's rule to the signals in it.

Privacy between participants is set by the ISN's permissions. For example, in a network where all participants share their data with a government agency but not with each other, the participants are given write-only access and the agency is given read access.

## Routing
Some networks have one ISN per destination, e.g. one per port. Instead of choosing the ISN yourself, you can send signals to the router (*Submit Signals via Router* or *Upload a Document via Router*), which chooses the ISN for each signal:
- **A signal with a `correlation_id`** goes to the ISN of the signal it is linked to.
- **A json signal without one** is matched against its signal type's routing rules, e.g. on a port code in its content. The rules are set up by the service administrators (see [/admin-docs](/admin-docs)).

The response gives the `isn_slug` each signal was sent to.

Combined with the searches across your ISNs (see *Searching*), this means your code doesn't need to know which ISNs exist: when a new port joins and your account is given access to its ISN, signals are routed to it and your searches find the responses.

## Batches, partial success and resending
Each request has a `batch_ref`: a label you choose to track your requests, e.g. one per scheduled run. Requests with the same `batch_ref` are added to the same batch, and *Get Batch Status* reports what was stored and what failed in it. The `batch_ref` doesn't affect how signals are stored.

Signals in a request are validated and stored one at a time: the valid signals are stored, and the ones that fail (e.g. content that doesn't match the schema, or an unknown `correlation_id`) are listed in the response with an error code. The response status tells you whether all, some or none of the signals were stored (see each endpoint).

Fix the failed signals and resend them in either of these ways:
- **Resend the whole request.** Signals that were already stored are returned with `unchanged: true`, and only the fixed signals are stored. Note that any json signal in the request that has been withdrawn since it was sent is reactivated (withdrawn events fail with `resource_already_exists`).
- **Resend only the failures.** *Get Batch Status* lists the batch's unresolved failures.

If the whole request fails (an error status such as 400, 401, 403, 404, 413 or 500), or you get no response, nothing is recorded in the batch, so resend the whole request once the problem is fixed. If the request times out partway through, the signals already stored stay stored and the rest are returned as `timeout` failures (not recorded in the batch). Resend the whole request, or just the signals that timed out.

# Searching
There are three search routes for private ISNs. The ISN and signal type in the path limit every filter, so e.g. a `local_ref` search on `consignment/v1.0.0` only finds consignments.

**One ISN, one signal type:**
```
GET /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search
```

**Every ISN you are a member of, one signal type:**
```
GET /api/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search
```

**Every ISN you are a member of, all signal types:**
```
GET /api/signals/search
```

Each result includes its `isn_slug`, `signal_type_slug` and `sem_ver`, so you can build further URLs from it (e.g. *Download a Document*). To search one ISN across all signal types, use `/api/signals/search` and filter the results on `isn_slug`.

Searches return the latest version of each signal. Use `include_previous_versions=true` to add earlier versions, `include_correlated=true` to add the signals linked to each result, and `include_withdrawn=true` to include withdrawn signals. The filters are described on each search endpoint.

## Polling for changes
To find out about new and changed signals, poll any of the search routes with `updated_since`, e.g.:
```
GET /api/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```
- `updated_since` returns the signals that changed (a new version was received, or the signal was withdrawn) since that time. Results are ordered by `signal_updated_at` across the ISNs searched, so the last result's `signal_updated_at` is your cursor.
- Use `include_withdrawn=true`, so withdrawn signals are returned with `is_withdrawn: true` (otherwise they silently drop out of the results).
- **Polling is at-least-once, so overlap your polls**: set `updated_since` to 1 minute before your cursor, and skip the results you have already seen (the same `signal_id` and `signal_updated_at`). `signal_updated_at` is set when the service starts storing a signal, not when it finishes, so a signal that was still being stored when you last polled can appear with a `signal_updated_at` a little before your cursor.
- Search results are not paginated, so poll often enough to keep each result set small.

## Following signals
**You received an event and need the signal it is about.** For example, an `ehc-approved` event is about a consignment, and you want the consignment with its documents and other events. The event's `correlation_id` is the consignment's `signal_id`:
```
GET /api/signals/search?signal_id={correlation_id}&include_correlated=true&include_withdrawn=true
```
The result is the consignment with everything linked to it (with `is_withdrawn: true` if it was withdrawn). The same search tells you what any `signal_id` is. Write-only accounts get an empty result if the consignment belongs to another account (see *Who can see signals*).

**You sent signals through the router and want the responses.** For example, you send consignments through the router, and the ports send back advice events linked to them. Poll the advice event type: the events from every port are returned, and each event's `correlation_id` is the `signal_id` the router returned for your consignment.
```
GET /api/signal-types/{advice_type}/v{sem_ver}/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```

**You keep a copy of the data.** For example, you store every consignment, and the documents and events linked to them. Poll every signal type, so you need one cursor rather than one per signal type:
```
GET /api/signals/search?updated_since={cursor}&include_withdrawn=true
```
- store each result by `signal_id`, and use its `correlation_id` to attach it to the signal it is linked to (a new version can change the `correlation_id`)
- a linked signal can arrive before the signal it is linked to, so keep it until that signal arrives
- signals of new signal types are returned too: skip the types you don't need

**You want to know when anything about one signal changes.** For example, you want an alert when a consignment gets a new version, or when a document or event is linked to it. Linking a signal changes the linked signal, not the consignment, so polling the consignment type with `updated_since` doesn't show new documents or events. Instead, poll the consignment with everything linked to it, and compare the result with the previous poll (there is no cursor to keep):
```
GET /api/signals/search?signal_id={signal_id}&include_correlated=true&include_withdrawn=true
```
- a new `signal_id`: a signal was linked to the consignment
- a different `signal_updated_at`: a new version, or a withdrawal (`is_withdrawn: true`)
- a missing `signal_id`: the signal was linked to a different signal (or can no longer be seen)

# Reference

## Error responses
All endpoints may return:
- `400` malformed request (invalid json, missing required fields, etc.)
- `401` unauthorized (invalid or expired credentials)
- `403` forbidden (insufficient permissions)
- `404` resource not found (e.g. an ISN or signal type that doesn't exist or is not in use)
- `413` request body exceeds the size limit
- `429` rate limit exceeded
- `500` internal server error
- `504` request timed out (`timeout`)

Error responses have a JSON body with `error_code`, `message` and `request_id` fields. The /oauth endpoints return `error` (the RFC 6749 error code), `error_code` and `error_description` instead. Individual endpoints document their specific errors.

## Request limits
- **Rate limit**: a configurable limit on requests per second, applied across all endpoints.
- **Request size** (configurable - these are the defaults): 64KB for admin and auth endpoints, 5MB for json and event submissions, 20MB for document uploads. The `Signalsd-Max-Request-Size` response header gives the limit for the endpoint called.

## Dates and times
Query parameters accept these ISO 8601 formats:
- `2006-01-02T15:04:05Z` (UTC)
- `2006-01-02T15:04:05+07:00` (with offset - encode the `+` as `%2B`, otherwise it may be read as a space)
- `2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999Z` (nanosecond precision)
- `2006-01-02` (date only, treated as the start of the day in UTC)

Dates and times in response bodies use RFC 3339, e.g. `2025-06-03T13:47:47.331787+01:00`.

## Browser apps
Browser-based apps on other sites can only call the public endpoints directly. The other endpoints have no CORS policy, so the browser won't send an access token to them or let the page read the response. Call the API from your app's backend (or a small proxy) instead - the "backend for frontend" pattern used by the signalsd UI. Server-side clients are not affected by CORS.

The refresh token cookie is HttpOnly and SameSite=Strict, and the server rejects POST, PUT and DELETE requests that the browser reports as coming from another origin. The other endpoints use bearer tokens, which browsers don't send automatically, so they are not open to CSRF.
info.title: Signals ISN API

post.description:
**Use Cases:**
- **Security Incident**: Compromised account needs immediate lockout
- **Employee Departure**: Remove access for departed staff

**Actions Performed:**
- Sets `is_active = false` (account becomes unusable)
- Revokes all client secrets/one-time secrets (service accounts)
- Revokes all refresh tokens (web users)

If an admin account is disables, it loses access to the admin endpoints straight away. Access tokens that were already issued remain valid on the other endpoints until they expire (up to 30 minutes).

**Recovery:** Account must be re-enabled by admin via `POST /api/admin/accounts/{account_id}/enable`
Service accounts will also need a new client secret via `/api/auth/service-accounts/reissue-credentials`

Only site admins can disable accounts (disabling an account removes its access to every ISN it belongs to).

ISN admins remove an account from their own ISN by revoking its ISN access.

**Administrative endpoint to re-enable previously disabled accounts.**
Sets account status to `is_active = true` (does not create new tokens).

**Post-Enable Steps Required:**
- **Service Accounts**: will need a new client secret via `/api/auth/service-accounts/reissue-credentials`
- **Web Users**: Can immediately log in again via `/api/auth/login`

Only site admins can enable accounts.

put.description:
This endpoint grants the ISN admin role to a site member

An ISN admin can:
- Create an ISN
- Add signal_types to their own ISNs
- read/write to their own ISNs
- Grant other accounts read or write access to their ISNs

Note that ISN admins can't change ISNs they don't own (a site admin must use the `transfer ownership` endpoint if this is required)

An ISN admin also has access to the following site-level functions:
- Create service accounts
- View all users and their email addresses

Account management (enabling and disabling accounts, password reset links and reissuing service account credentials) is done by site admins, since it affects the account on every ISN it belongs to.

The admin endpoints use the new role straight away. The UI shows or hides the admin pages when the account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

**This endpoint can only be used by site admin accounts**

delete.description:
The account reverts to the member role.

The admin endpoints use the new role straight away. The UI shows or hides the admin pages when the account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

**This endpoint can only be used by site admin accounts**

put.description:
This endpoint grants the site admin role to a user.

A site admin can create and manage any ISN and administer accounts on the site.

The following tasks can only be performed by site admins:
- Create new signal types on the site
- Register new signal type schemas
- Transfer ISN ownership between accounts
- Assign the site admin role to other users

The admin endpoints use the new role straight away. The UI shows or hides the admin pages when the account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

**This endpoint can only be used by site admin accounts**

delete.description:
The account reverts to the member role.

The admin endpoints use the new role straight away. The UI shows or hides the admin pages when the account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

**This endpoint can only be used by site admin accounts**

put.description:
Transfer ownership of an ISN to another admin account.
This can be used when an admin leaves or when reorganizing responsibilities.
Only site admins can transfer ISN ownership.

post.description:
Delete all registered users, signal types and associated data.
This endpoint only works on environments configured as 'dev'

get.description:
Only site admins and ISN admins can view service account lists.

To return a specific service account supply one of the following query parameter combinations:
-	id (account ID)
-	client_id
-	client_email & client_organization

No query parameters = return all service accounts

parameters.description: Service Account Contact Email (must be used with client_organization)
parameters.name: client_email

parameters.description: Service Account Organization (must be used with client_email)
parameters.name: client_organization

200.description: Specific service account (when query params provided)

get.description:
Get details for all the signal types registered on the site.

Use GET /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types to get the signal types that have been added to an ISN.

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

post.description:
Signal types specify a record that can be shared on the site
- The title is used to create a URL-friendly slug, which must be unique for the site (two titles that produce the same slug conflict - 409)
- The title and slug fields can't be changed
- The signal type fields are defined in an external JSON schema file and this schema file is used to validate signals before loading

Content kinds
- json (default): signals are JSON validated against the signal type's schema
- document: signals are files (e.g. a PDF bill of lading) Document signal types do not have a schema - omit schema_url
- event: signals are immutable JSON records of a process waypoint (e.g. export health certificate approved), validated against the signal type's schema.
Events must be correlated to the signal they are about and have an occurred_at timestamp in their content (see Submit Signals)

JSON Schema URL Requirements
- Must be a link to a schema file on a public github repo (e.g., https://github.com/org/repo/blob/main/sample-signal-type/2025-01-01/schema.json)
- To disable schema validation, use the special URL: https://github.com/skip/validation/main/schema.json

Readme URL requirements
- Must be a link to a file ending .md on a public github repo.
- Use the special URL: https://github.com/skip/readme/main/readme.md to indicate there is no readme

Versions
- A signal type can have multiple versions - these share the same title/slug but have different JSON schemas
- Use this endpoint to create the first version - the bump_type (major/minor/patch) determines the initial semver (1.0.0, 0.1.0 or 0.0.1)

After creating a signal type, use the AddSignalTypeToIsn endpoint to link it to one or more ISNs.

Signal type definitions are referred to in paths like this: {signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver} (e.g. /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver})

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

Registers a new schema for an existing signal type

You must specify a schema_url that has not been previously registered for this signal type.

Use the bump_type (major/minor/patch) parameter to determine how the version number should be incremented.

The new version keeps the title and content_kind of the existing signal type.
Schemas can only be registered for json and event signal types.

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

get.description:
Returns the signal type details.

Use GET /api/isn/{isn_slug}/signal-types/{signal_type_slug}/v{sem_ver} to see how a signal type is used on an ISN.

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

put.description:
Update the description or link to the readme file

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

parameters.description: signal type details to be updated
parameters.name: request

delete.description:
Only signal types that have never been referenced by signals can be deleted.

Deleting a signal type also removes it from every ISN it was added to, and deletes its routing config.

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

get.description: Returns the Signals Routing Rules for a signal type.

put.description:
Replaces the route config for the specified signal type path

the routing_field must be a plain Dot Notation path that is defined in the signal type's schema -
field names can only contain letters, digits, '_', '-', ':' and '@' (e.g. JSON-LD keys such as location.@value) and are always matched literally.
Empty path segments and numeric (array index) path segments are not allowed.

When using the 'matches' and 'does_not_match' operators, any occurrence of '*' and '?' in the matching pattern will be treated as a wildcard ('equals' and 'does_not_equal' compare the pattern literally).
The pattern is always compared to the full contents of the specified routing field.

Patterns are matched in order according to the supplied sequence number (smallest sequence first)
and the first match is accepted. Each rule must have a different sequence number.
Where the routing field is an array, the rule matches if one or more elements match
(for 'does_not_match' and 'does_not_equal', if one or more elements do not match the pattern).

The new config is used immediately by the instance that handled the request, and by the other instances of the service within 30 seconds.

delete.description: Removes all routing information for a signal type version.

post.description:
Updates the schema of an existing signal type version in place, without creating a new version: the schema file is fetched again from the signal type's schema_url.

The schema is stored when the signal type version is registered, so changes to the schema file on GitHub are not used until the schema is refreshed.
To change the schema, update the file on GitHub (GitHub keeps the history of the file) and then call this endpoint.

Use with caution - replacing a schema with an incompatible version will break existing integrations - if in doubt, register a new schema instead and ask clients to migrate.

As a safety check, the most recent 1000 signal versions are validated against the new schema.

If the signal type has a routing config, the routing field must be defined in the new schema.

Schemas can only be replaced for json and event signal types.

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins

get.description:
This api displays site users and their email addresses (can only be used by admin accounts)

- No query parameters = return all users
- to return a specific user supply one of the following query parameters: `?id=uuid` or `?email=address`

post.description:
Allows admins to generate a one-time password reset link for a user (use this endpoint when a user has forgotten their password)

Send the `reset_url` from the response to the user. Opening it in a browser serves the password reset form (see *Password Reset Form* under One-time Links), where they can choose a new password.
The link expires in 30 minutes and can only be used once. Generating a new link for a user invalidates any link they were issued previously.

Only site admins can generate links, since the link resets the account's password on every ISN it belongs to.

**Note:** anyone in possession of the link can reset the password of the associated account. The link should be treated as sensitive and handled accordingly.

The response body includes an access token which can be used to access the protected endpoints, assuming the account has the appropriate permissions.
The access_token is valid for 30 minutes.

As part of the login response, the server sets a http-only cookie on the client that will allow it to refresh the token (POST to the /oauth/token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token in the form body).
The cookie's path is `/oauth`, so browsers only send it to the /oauth endpoints.
The refresh_token lasts 30 days unless it is revoked earlier.
- Each refresh issues a new refresh_token valid for another 30 days, so the user only has to log in again if they don't refresh for 30 days.
- Logging in revokes the user's other refresh tokens, so a user has one active session at a time.
- To revoke the refresh_token, call the /oauth/revoke endpoint.

The account's role and permissions are encoded as part of the jwt access token and this information is also provided in the response body.

get.description:
Serves the HTML form a user fills in to choose a new password after an admin has issued them a reset link.

This is the page a user lands on when they open the link returned by *Generate Password Reset Link* (Account Management).

The `token_id` in the URL is validated before the form is rendered. The form then posts the new password back to the same URL (see *Submit New Password*).

Reset links expire 30 minutes after they are generated and can only be used once.

parameters.description: Password reset token ID, taken from the reset link
parameters.name: token_id

400.description: HTML error page - if the token is unknown, already used or expired the endpoint returns 400 with an HTML body.

post.description:
Sets a new password using a one-time reset token, then consumes the token.

This is the submission target of the form served by *Password Reset Form* at the same URL, posted by the form's own JavaScript.

On success the token is deleted so the link can't be reused, the user's existing sessions are ended (their refresh tokens are revoked), and the user can log in with the new password.

Note that no access token is required - possession of the reset token is what authorises the change. Reset tokens can only be issued by site admins (see *Generate Password Reset Link* in the admin API docs).

parameters.description: Password reset token ID, taken from the reset link
parameters.name: token_id

put.description:
Changes the password of the signed-in user.

The caller must supply a valid access token and their current password. The new password must be at least 11 characters.

On success all the user's sessions are ended (their refresh tokens are revoked), including the current one, so they will need to log in again when their access token expires.

Users who have forgotten their password can't use this endpoint, since they have no current password to supply - an admin has to issue them a one-time reset link instead (see *Generate Password Reset Link* in the admin API docs).

post.description:
Registers a web user with an email address and a password.

The first user created is granted the "siteadmin" role and has super-user access to the site. Everyone who registers after that gets the "member" role.
New members can't access any information beyond the public data on the site until an admin grants them access to an ISN.

Site admins can grant other users the "isnadmin" role.
ISN admins can create ISNs and service accounts, and grant other accounts permission to read or write to the ISNs they own.

Registering a new service account creates a one-time setup link. Send it to whoever is operating the service account - opening it in a browser shows them their client credentials. The link expires after 48 hours and can only be used once.

Note that where an organization needs more than one service account they must supply unique contact emails for each account.

To reissue credentials for an existing service account, use the **Reissue Service Account Credentials** endpoint.

Only site admins and ISN admins can use this endpoint

Reissue credentials for an existing service account.
This creates a new one-time setup link carrying fresh client credentials. Send it to whoever operates the service account - opening it in a browser shows them the new credentials (see *Service Account Setup Page* under One-time Links). The link expires after 48 hours and can only be used once.

This endpoint revokes all existing client secrets and one-time setup URLs for the service account, then generates new credentials.

The client_id will remain the same, but a new client_secret will be generated.

Only site admins can use this endpoint.

get.description:
Exchanges a one-time setup ID for client credentials and renders an HTML page where the user can copy them.

This is the page reached by opening the link returned by *Register Service Account* or *Reissue Service Account Credentials*.

Setup links expire 48 hours after they are issued and can only be used once - opening the page consumes the setup ID and revokes any client secret the service account was previously using. The client secret shown on the page is valid for one year and is not recoverable afterwards, so it has to be copied at this point.

parameters.description: One-time setup ID, taken from the setup link
parameters.name: setup_id

201.description: HTML page displaying the client_id and client_secret

400.description: HTML error page - if the token is unknown, already used or expired the endpoint returns 400 with an HTML body.

post.description:
Create an Information Sharing Network (ISN)

*Visibility*
Signals in a private ISN can only be seen by members of the ISN.
Signals in a public ISN can be viewed by anyone (no authentication required).
Accounts need write permission for the ISN before they can submit signals

Once the ISN is created you can:
- Grant accounts permission to use it
- Add the Signal Types that can be shared over the network

There can be multiple ISNs on the site and each ISN can have a
different membership and be configured for different Signal Types.

This endpoint can only be used by ISN admins and site admins

All fields (title, detail, is_in_use and visibility) are required.

put.description:
Update the ISN configuration
This endpoint can only be used by admin accounts
ISN admins can only update ISNs they own
Site admins can update any ISN

get.description:
Get a list of all accounts (users and service accounts) that have had permissions on the specified ISN.
Accounts whose access has been revoked are included (with can_read and can_write both false).
Only ISN admins (for the ISNs they own) and site admins can view this information

put.description:
Update an account's access permission for an ISN. Set both can_read and can_write to false to revoke all access.

This endpoint can only be used by admin accounts:
- ISN admins can only update membership for ISNs they own.
- Site admins can update membership for any ISN

Permissions:
- Accounts with 'read' permission can view all signals on the ISN.
- Accounts with 'write' permission can create signals on the ISN.
- For accounts that need read/write access to an ISN, you must grant both 'read' and 'write' permissions.

Note that accounts with only 'write' permission to an ISN can view the signals they created, and the signals other accounts have correlated to their signals, but no others.

The change takes effect when the account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

You must supply values for both can_read and can_write.

post.description:
Link an existing signal type to an ISN

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins and ISN admins.
ISN admins can only add signal types to ISNs they own.

Adding a signal type that is already on the ISN does nothing.
post.summary: Add a Signal Type to an ISN

put.description:
Enable or disable a signal type for a specific ISN

When a signal type is disabled for an ISN, signals of this type can no longer be read or written to the ISN.
The change takes effect when each account next gets an access token (up to 30 minutes later).

Note: this endpoint can only be used by site admins and ISN admins.
ISN admins can only update signal types for ISNs they own.

Check if the signalsd service is ready to accept traffic.

post.description:
Revokes credentials to prevent them being used to obtain new access tokens.
The request body must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (RFC 6749).
Any access tokens already issued remain valid until they expire (30 minutes).

---

**Service Accounts — `client_credentials` grant (logout / credential rotation)**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=client_credentials`
- `client_id=<your_client_id>`
- `client_secret=<your_client_secret>`

Alternatively, credentials may be supplied via HTTP Basic Auth (`Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)`).

Revokes **all** client secrets for the service account, which prevents any further token requests
until an admin reissues credentials via `POST /api/auth/service-accounts/reissue-credentials`.
This does not permanently disable the account — use `POST /api/admin/accounts/{account_id}/disable` for that.

---

**Web Users — `refresh_token` grant (logout)**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=refresh_token`

The refresh token is read automatically from the `refresh_token` HTTP-only cookie.
No additional form fields are required.

Revokes the current refresh token. The user must log in again to obtain a new one.

400.description: unsupported_grant_type · invalid_request · invalid_grant (refresh token missing, expired or revoked - error_code refresh_token_invalid)

post.description:
Issues a new access token. The request body must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` (RFC 6749).

Service accounts use the `client_credentials` grant, web users use the `refresh_token` grant - see below.

---

**Service Accounts — `client_credentials` grant**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=client_credentials`
- `client_id=<your_client_id>`
- `client_secret=<your_client_secret>`

Alternatively, credentials may be supplied via HTTP Basic Auth (`Authorization: Basic base64(client_id:client_secret)`).

Returns a new access token in the response body. Access tokens expire after 30 minutes.

---

**Web Users — `refresh_token` grant**

Include in the request body:
- `grant_type=refresh_token`

The refresh token is read automatically from the `refresh_token` HTTP-only cookie set during login.
No additional form fields are required.

Returns a new access token in the response body. The rotated refresh token is set as a new HTTP-only cookie
(the cookie's path is `/oauth`, so browsers only send it to the /oauth endpoints).
Access tokens expire after 30 minutes. Each refresh issues a new refresh token that expires 30 days later,
so the user only has to log in again if they don't refresh for 30 days. Refreshing revokes the user's other refresh tokens (one session per user).
